facts.raw_span: A man in his 30s presented with a mass in the right nostril that had been growing for about 1 year
The lesion bled with minimal trauma but did not obstruct his breathing
The patient did not smoke and denied any medical history of chronic rhinosinusitis
Physical examination revealed a 1-cm, nontender, exophytic, verrucous, skin-colored plaque on the right nasal vestibule
Papillary fronds with slender fibrovascular cores that are lined by nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium
Shows mucin-containing goblet cells
Neither cytologic atypia nor atypical mitotic figures are present
An exophytic, verrucous, and skin-colored plaque on the right nasal vestibule

concepts.why: The presence of a 1-cm, exophytic, verrucous, skin-colored plaque on the right nasal vestibule, along with histologic examination showing papillary fronds with slender fibrovascular cores lined by nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium and mucin-containing goblet cells, is consistent with inverted papilloma.

The lesion's tendency to bleed with minimal trauma and its exophytic, verrucous appearance, although not definitive, raise the possibility of squamous cell carcinoma, especially given the patient's age and the location of the lesion.

The patient's presentation with a mass in the right nostril that has been growing for about 1 year, without a history of chronic rhinosinusitis, could suggest a nasal vestibular furuncle, although the histologic findings do not support this diagnosis.
The exophytic, verrucous appearance of the lesion, combined with the absence of cytologic atypia or atypical mitotic figures, could suggest verrucous carcinoma, a low-grade malignancy.

The histologic findings of papillary fronds with slender fibrovascular cores lined by nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium are consistent with a papilloma, although the specific type (e.g., inverted papilloma) is more likely given the clinical context.

The presence of a mass in the right nostril could suggest a nasal polyp, although the histologic examination does not support this diagnosis, and the absence of a history of chronic rhinosinusitis makes it less likely.

The exophytic, verrucous appearance of the lesion, although not typical, could suggest keratoacanthoma, a low-grade malignancy that can resemble squamous cell carcinoma, but the histologic findings do not fully support this diagnosis.
The skin-colored plaque on the right nasal vestibule could suggest seborrheic keratosis, a benign growth, although the histologic examination does not support this diagnosis.
